title: Who Is Pawan Kumar Chandana? The Former ISRO Scientist Who Just Made India a Private Space Power

body:
On July 18, 2026, a 22-metre rocket built in Hyderabad lifted off from Sriharikota and placed payloads into a 450-kilometre orbit. Fifteen minutes of flight time put India in a club of three — the only nations where a private company, not a government agency, has sent a rocket into orbit. Behind that rocket, Vikram-1, and the company that built it, Skyroot Aerospace, stands Pawan Kumar Chandana — a 35-year-old whose own journey to the launchpad is almost as improbable as the mission itself.

From 51 Marks to IIT Kharagpur

Chandana was born in 1991 into a middle-class family in Hyderabad. By his own telling, he was not an obviously gifted student. He once scored just 51 out of 100 in a school mathematics exam — a result that might have closed the door on engineering before it opened. But his father refused to give up, enrolling him in IIT-JEE coaching. Something in those sessions rewired how Chandana related to numbers. A subject he had feared became one he was drawn to.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=tM42lU5Glp0

He cleared the IIT entrance exam on his first attempt in 2007, joining IIT Kharagpur for a dual degree — a B.Tech in Mechanical Engineering and an M.Tech in Thermal Engineering — which he completed by 2012.

The ISRO Years

While many of his batchmates took campus placements in the tech industry or headed abroad, Chandana joined the Indian Space Research Organisation straight out of college. Over nearly six years at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre in Thiruvananthapuram, he worked on the GSLV Mk-III — India’s heaviest launch vehicle — served as a systems engineer on the S200 solid booster of the GSLV Mk-II, and later became deputy project manager on the Small Satellite Launch Vehicle programme. His work earned him two internal ISRO innovation awards.

“I believe rockets are the most fascinating machinery ever built by humans, and are now in need of a new techno-economic makeover to open up a new frontier in space access and exploration.”

By 2018, Chandana had concluded that India’s space programme needed a private-sector counterpart — one that could build and launch rockets faster and cheaper than a government agency constrained by long procurement cycles and limited launch windows.

A LinkedIn Message That Changed Everything

Leaving ISRO meant walking away from job security with no business background, no investor network, and no guarantee that India’s regulations would even permit a private rocket company to operate. What Chandana did have was an IIT Kharagpur alumni network and a LinkedIn account.

He used it to cold-message Mukesh Bansal, the entrepreneur behind Myntra, CureFit, and Nurix — and a fellow IIT Kharagpur graduate. Bansal backed him with $1.5 million. Skyroot Aerospace was born in June 2018, with Naga Bharath Daka, a fellow ex-ISRO engineer and IIT Bombay graduate, joining as co-founder and COO.

The early years were brutal. The COVID-19 pandemic froze fundraising just as Skyroot needed capital. The founders of renewable energy giant Greenko stepped in to keep the company alive. Gradually, marquee global investors followed — GIC, Temasek, and others — pushing the valuation to roughly $1.1 billion and making Skyroot India’s first space-sector unicorn.

Vikram-S to Vikram-1: The Road to Orbit

Skyroot’s vehicles are named after Vikram Sarabhai, the founder of India’s space programme. The first milestone came in November 2022, when Vikram-S — an all-carbon-composite suborbital rocket — flew successfully under Mission Prarambh, becoming India’s first privately built rocket to reach space.

But orbit was a different challenge entirely. Vikram-1, a three-stage solid-fuel rocket topped by a liquid-fuelled orbit adjustment module, required developing entirely new systems in-house — from the Raman-1 solid rocket engine to the Dhawan-1 cryogenic engine, each needing its own static-fire test before flight.

On July 18, 2026, under Mission Aagaman, Vikram-1 lifted off and achieved orbit on its maiden attempt — a textbook success that exceeded even industry expectations. The average age of the team that built it was just 28. Prime Minister Narendra Modi placed a personal congratulatory call to Chandana and Daka shortly after.

Why He Matters Now

Vikram-1’s success is not just a corporate milestone. It signals that India’s post-2020 space liberalisation — opening the sector to private players through agencies like IN-SPACe — is producing results. Skyroot now employs more than 1,000 people, operates two campuses in Hyderabad, and is developing Vikram-II, a larger cryogenic-powered rocket expected to fly in 2027 with nearly triple the payload capacity.

Chandana was named to the Forbes 30 Under 30 Asia list in 2020. He married Nirupama Tungala in October 2019. He has spoken publicly about wanting to make launching a satellite as routine as booking a commercial flight — a vision that now, for the first time, has a flight-proven rocket behind it.

For India’s space ecosystem and for the global small-satellite market watching from the sidelines, the question is no longer whether Indian startups can build orbital rockets. Thanks to a Hyderabad boy who once scored 51 in maths, the question is how fast they can do it again.
